Please review the manuscript in /papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/, the previous chat handoff research-progress/handoffs/HDA-A01-AN01.md, and the research summary ansatz/notes/07_CHAT0001_RESEARCH_SUMMARY_20261025.md, in addition to the research-overview and progress files. 

Please discuss at a high level what has been accomplished in the last round of research, and how it fits in with the overall research program.
I’ll read the manuscript, handoff, and research summaries, then explain what the latest results establish and how they fit into the broader program.

The original handoff was followed by three further research steps. The latest summary records controlled approximations through zero heat time and across the negative interval \([-2,0]\), with derivative bounds. I’m checking how these field results connect to the density and covariance goals that remain open.

The broader program already has a finite analytical construction covering all time and height. This branch is developing more informative large-height formulas with controlled amplitude, phase, and arithmetic corrections. The strongest new milestone is joining the near-zero and negative-time formulas while explicitly bounding the errors introduced by that join.

The remaining gap is the transfer from accurate field formulas to the program’s nonlinear density, current, and covariance quantities. The negative-time construction also still contains a growing arithmetic sum and a correction integral, so its strong error bound has not yet delivered the short formula or useful evaluation cost sought by the program.

**The last round made substantial progress toward a controlled large-height description of the heat field. Its strongest milestone is a joined approximation covering the entire negative-time interval \([-2,0]\), with spatial and time derivatives controlled.** It also established the first corrected positive-time formula and resolved the arithmetic crossover through zero.

The original HDA-A01-AN01 handoff captures only the beginning of this work. Its unresolved complex-remainder estimate was subsequently closed, followed by two negative-time continuations. The [research summary](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/notes/07_CHAT0001_RESEARCH_SUMMARY_20261025.md) and current progress register therefore give a substantially stronger picture than the original handoff alone.

The four main accomplishments are:

1. **The positive-time cosine now has a justified first correction.** On \(32\le t\le33\), the work pins down the amplitude, phase, and normalization, including contributions from the displaced saddle and Gaussian determinant. These corrections are compared with the actual canonical field, with the arithmetic remainder included. This makes the formula a quantitative approximation within its stated domain.

2. **The arithmetic structure is controlled through zero time.** Near \(t=0\), a single cosine is insufficient: the growing Riemann–Siegel sum and its correction matter. The work establishes a corrected finite-sum comparison on
   \[
   |t|\log(X/(4\pi))\le8,
   \]
   including complex neighborhoods large enough for the intended averaging and differentiation. Closing that complex-domain gap supplies spatial derivatives through order three and a direct first time derivative.

3. **Fixed negative times now have two clearly distinguished representations.** A relatively short formula is accurate on the natural gamma scale. Achieving accuracy against the smaller outer envelope requires a more elaborate construction, with growing expansion orders and a retained correction integral. This identifies an important tradeoff: strong accuracy has been obtained, while the desired short formula remains an open simplification problem.

4. **The negative-time formulas have been joined with their errors accounted for.** The construction extends toward zero and overlaps with the crossover formula. The resulting approximation covers \([-2,0]\), with field error bounded by \(C X^{-1/4}\) times a positive carrier envelope, and derivative errors carrying specified logarithmic factors. The extra time-derivative and heat-equation errors introduced by joining the formulas are explicitly retained. These results are incorporated in the [maintained manuscript](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/manuscript/main.tex).

**Its role in the broader program is to improve the quality and explanatory power of the representation.** The parent investigation already records a finite analytical construction covering all real time and height, together with subsequent improvements in source compression and evaluation cost. The ansatz branch addresses a further requirement: formulas that reveal the large-height amplitude, phase, arithmetic contributions, and changes between regimes. That distinction is explicit in the [parent research overview](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/research-overview/01_AVERAGED_DENSITY_RESEARCH_PROGRAM_20261024.md).

This matters because the ultimate target is the smoothed density and its evolution, including current and actual signed covariance. Accurate field derivatives provide necessary inputs to those quantities. **Transferring the new approximations to those nonlinear observables remains unfinished**, especially where the regulator and small field values amplify errors. The parent’s existing observable results remain available; the new ansatz formulas need their own transfer estimates.

Within the wider RH program, this develops quantitative tools for the canonical xi heat flow studied in the [Polymath work](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12438). It continues the repository’s productive emphasis on retaining arithmetic corrections and proving stronger remainder bounds, recorded in the [heat-flow result summary](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/result-summaries/11_newman_heat_flow_reductions_and_certificates.md). The gains meet the project’s [quantitative-progress standard](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/avoid/01_restating_the_target.md), but establish no new RH, simplicity, collision-exclusion, or Newman-bound conclusion.

The next prepared task—[HDA-A03-AN01](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/research-progress/handoffs/HDA-A03-AN01.md)—addresses the regulator transition near \(t=64\): how improved amplitude formulas change its comparison center relative to its very narrow rounding width. This is a separate phenomenon from the arithmetic crossover near zero; the switch at 64 belongs to the chosen measurement protocol.

The remaining major obligations are broader time coverage and matching, physical-observable transfer, useful evaluation cost, and independent review. Accordingly, A01 is complete at its bounded scope, A02 remains partial, and the parent statuses remain HDA-17 **Partial**, HDA-18 **Gated**, and HDA-20 **unfulfilled**. The new results carry “proved in-note from named classical inputs” status with same-model internal assessments and unevaluated onset constants; this high-level review does not replace the outstanding full-chain audit.

How much has the evolution equation been used for these ansatz? Is there a formula that applies the evolution equations to the ansatz with the error terms, and attempts to derive the evolution equations acting on the ansatz? This could be done asymptotically - perhaps it could help with the issue in 3, trying to understand how the intermediate times look at negative time. 

I agree that understanding the transition near t=64 is also important. The goal is to understand all of it as well as possible, with an emphasis on the asymptotics at large height.

I’ll check how the manuscript uses the heat equation and the density evolution equations, then assess whether a direct asymptotic evolution calculation could clarify the intermediate negative-time regime.

The equation has been used substantially: the notes compute each ansatz’s heat residual, use it to control time derivatives, and construct a negative-time model that solves the heat equation exactly. The parent work also has explicit residual-forcing terms for the density and current equations. The opportunity you identify is to use these equations more directly to construct and simplify the asymptotic formulas.

Rewriting the negative-time formula makes the mechanism clearer: each arithmetic mode acquires the damping factor \(e^{-T k_n^2}\), where \(T=-t\) and \(k_n=\tfrac14\log(X/(4\pi))-\tfrac12\log n\). The modes therefore evolve at different rates. I’m recording this interpretation and the exact residual-forcing formulas, while keeping the harder question—controlling cancellation across the full sum—explicitly open.

There is also an exact equation for the approximation error, driven by the ansatz’s heat residual. In negative time it can be written using forward heat propagation. The key unresolved step is to control that propagation relative to the very small large-height envelope; an ordinary absolute error bound can be insufficient. I’m saving a bounded continuation that tests this approach without replacing the \(t=64\) work.

**The evolution equation has already been used substantially, and your suggestion identifies a useful further application: use it systematically to construct and simplify the asymptotic formulas.** My earlier summary understated the existing evolution work.

There are three distinct uses already present:

- **Construction:** the more elaborate negative-time representation in Note05 solves the heat equation exactly on each fixed spatial chart.
- **Correction and error control:** Notes03–04 calculate the ansatz’s heat residual, cancel its leading terms, and combine it with spatial error estimates to obtain time-derivative estimates.
- **Observable evolution:** the parent investigation already derives equations for an approximate field’s density, potential, current and covariance, including explicit forcing from its heat residual. Those formulas are in [Note31, PE33–39](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/notes/31_POSITIVE_ALL_HEIGHT_EVOLUTION_AND_COVARIANCE_20261024.md).

What remains less developed is using that machinery to produce a **shorter, systematically corrected negative-time description**.

For an ansatz \(F\), the basic formulation is particularly clean. Define its heat residual and approximation error by
\[
\mathfrak r_F=F_t+F_{zz},\qquad E=H-F.
\]
Then the error satisfies the exact forced equation
\[
\boxed{E_t+E_{zz}=-\mathfrak r_F.}
\]
This explicitly separates errors in the initial approximation from errors in its subsequent evolution.

At negative time, put \(T=-t\). The true field then satisfies ordinary forward heat diffusion. Writing \(f(T,z)=F(-T,z)\) and \(d=f_T-f_{zz}\), the corresponding error formula is
\[
E(T)=\mathsf S_{T-T_0}E(T_0)
-\int_{T_0}^{T}\mathsf S_{T-s}d(s)\,ds,
\]
where \(\mathsf S_v\) is Gaussian heat propagation. This is the standard [Duhamel formula](https://web.stanford.edu/class/math220b/handouts/heateqn.pdf), under the appropriate function-space assumptions.

**That is a promising route for constructing corrections and proving their effects.** The remaining analytical obligation is to control this propagation on the relevant large-height scale, including complex buffers and tails. An ordinary absolute error bound can still be much larger than the exponentially small outer envelope.

There is also a direct amplitude-and-phase version of your proposal. For a chosen nonvanishing complex arm
\[
f(T,x)=a(T,x)e^{i\theta(T,x)},
\]
the exact heat equation gives
\[
\boxed{
a_T=a_{xx}-a\theta_x^2,\qquad
\theta_T=\theta_{xx}+2\frac{a_x}{a}\theta_x.
}
\]
An approximate arm has explicit forcing terms on the right, obtained from its residual. We can insert asymptotic expansions for \(a\) and \(\theta\), solve successive correction equations, and then estimate the remainder. These equations apply to the individual arms; they do not require dividing by the real field at its zeros.

This perspective already makes the intermediate negative-time formula more intelligible. Set
\[
L=\log(X/(4\pi)),\qquad
k_n=\frac L4-\frac12\log n.
\]
The existing short ansatz’s mode amplitudes can be rewritten **exactly** as
\[
A_o(-T,X)w_n(-T,X)
=A_o(0,X)n^{-1/2}e^{\pi^2T/64}e^{-Tk_n^2}.
\]
Its phase also receives the explicit shift \(-\pi T k_n/4\). Thus the formula describes heat filtering of a family of arithmetic frequencies:

- Fixed low-index modes have frequencies of order \(\log X\), so negative-time evolution strongly damps them.
- Modes near the Riemann–Siegel cutoff have smaller frequencies and survive longer.
- The surviving population still grows with height, and cancellation between its terms and the correction remains important.

This helps explain why intermediate negative times are difficult to compress into one amplitude and phase. It also clarifies the two error scales in my earlier point 3: the outer carrier can become extremely small while a natural-scale approximation still carries a substantially larger allowance. The rewriting inherits the existing error bounds; it does not establish which terms dominate the actual signed field.

For the density equations, the residual has an equally explicit role. With
\[
U_F=K*\log(|F|^2+q),
\]
the exact potential evolution contains the extra forcing
\[
\boxed{
K*\Xi_F,\qquad
\Xi_F=\frac{2\operatorname{Re}(\overline F\,\mathfrak r_F)}
{|F|^2+q}.
}
\]
The density equation consequently contains \(\Delta(K*\Xi_F)/(4\pi)\), alongside the actual covariance and regulator corrections. So the requested “evolution equations acting on the ansatz with error terms” already exist. The outstanding work is to obtain sufficiently informative asymptotic bounds for their terms.

One important limitation guides the next step: **the elaborate negative-time model already has zero heat residual.** Its complexity comes from representing the canonical arithmetic initial data accurately. Further simplification must exploit that structure and its cancellations, while preserving the initial-error estimate.

I saved these formulas and their scope in [Note08](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/notes/08_EVOLUTION_RESIDUAL_AND_NEGATIVE_TIME_MODES_20261025.md), and prepared a complementary [HDA-A02-AN03 handoff](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/research-progress/handoffs/HDA-A02-AN03.md). The next deliverable is **Analysis — Sol**: derive one explicit evolution correction on the existing fixed negative-time interval, prove an actual improvement, and compare its natural and outer error scales.

The \(t\approx64\) packet remains intact. Together, these address two parts of your larger objective: how the arithmetic field evolves at large height, and how that field interacts with the regulator to produce the observed density transition.

Please rewrite the manuscript with this perspective in mind. Please create a new research-overview note that prioritizes goals based on this perspective, with a corresponding research-progress note, within the ansatz folder. I think understanding the t=64 behavior is still important, but I would prioritize understanding and bounding the asymptotic estimates that you've outlined here to be top priority, for all times. Please verify the chat history within the ansatz folder.

I’ll rewrite the manuscript around evolution-driven asymptotics, make that the top priority across all time regimes, and retain the \(t=64\) transition as a supporting workstream. I’ll also create the new overview and progress notes and verify this chat’s archive in the ansatz folder.

I’m using the PDF skill to check the rewritten manuscript’s layout. The new overview and progress note will become the current planning documents, with the earlier pair retained as historical records. I’ll preserve the distinction between established estimates, exact identities, and proposed proof methods.

The existing work already uses heat evolution to construct the negative-time models and calculate their defects. I’m making the next step explicit: use those defects to build corrections, then prove bounds for the actual approximation error. The revised plan will distinguish fixed times, uniform compact intervals, and joint time–height limits so that “all times” has a precise scope.

The revised manuscript now has a central section on the error equation, amplitude and phase corrections, and the stability needed to turn a small residual into a useful bound. The negative-time discussion also separates the damping of individual modes from the behavior of the complete signed sum; that distinction is essential when many modes remain near the cutoff.

Both ansatz chat archives passed the integrity checks: their stored hashes, message counts, identities, provenance, and public transcript contents match, and each has one registration. The new planning pair makes the negative-time correction the next bounded task while keeping positive-time coverage and joint limits in the top priority. The prepared \(t=64\) packet is retained as supporting work.

The manuscript compiles without warnings after correcting one long equation. I’m checking the rendered pages and cross-references now, and confirming that the rewrite preserves the earlier bounded estimates and keeps proposed improvements clearly marked as unproved.

The rewrite and new planning notes are complete. The final PDF is 26 pages, compiles without warnings, and has passed the layout check. The earlier mathematical displays and proposition statements are preserved; the new material explains the evolution framework and proof obligations without presenting the proposed error improvements as established results.

Rewritten around **evolution equations and controlled large-height asymptotics across all times**, with \(t=64\) retained as supporting work. The manuscript now develops error evolution, correction equations, negative-time arithmetic modes, and explicit observable forcing.
